subject: cicada
title: A Fungus Eats a Third of This Insect, Then Drugs It to Keep Flying

scenes.text: This cicada is missing a third of its body. It hasn't noticed.
A fungus has eaten its abdomen and genitals and replaced them with a chalky white plug of spores.
It should be dead. Instead it keeps flying and trying to mate, as if nothing happened.
Because the fungus is drugging it. Scientists found an amphetamine inside infected cicadas, and in some, psilocybin from magic mushrooms.
Infected males even flick their wings like females, luring healthy males in. Every touch spreads the spores.
Researchers call them flying salt shakers of death. In some areas, one cicada in four is one.

description:
The fungus Massospora consumes a cicada's abdomen and genitals, more than a third of its body, and replaces them with a plug of spores, yet the insect keeps flying and trying to mate.
West Virginia University researchers found cathinone, an amphetamine, in infected cicadas and psilocybin in some, chemicals that appear to keep the hosts active. Infected males mimic female wing-flicks to attract healthy males, spreading the spores; in some areas 20 to 30 percent of cicadas are infected. It cannot infect people.
Is this the creepiest fungus in nature? Comment below.
thumbnail_text: A FUNGUS ATE ITS REAR END
first_comment: The fungus is harmless to people and pets; the drug doses are tiny. Overall fewer than 5 percent of cicadas carry it, but hotspots hit 20 to 30 percent. Which parasite should we cover next?
